title: Calcium Feedback Sets Photoreceptor Gain, and When Photoreceptors Die

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Photoreceptor {{c1::gain}} is how much current one absorbed photon switches off, and for how long.
cards.quote: Gain is how much current one absorbed photon switches off, and for how long.
cards.section: Why a photoreceptor must turn its own gain down

cards.front: Photoreceptor flash sensitivity equals the response to a dim flash divided by {{c1::the strength of that flash}}.
cards.quote: Sensitivity is the response to a dim flash divided by the strength of that flash.
cards.section: Why a photoreceptor must turn its own gain down

cards.front: Visual contrast is a change in light expressed as {{c1::a fraction of the background}}.
cards.quote: Contrast is a change in light as a fraction of the background.
cards.section: Why a photoreceptor must turn its own gain down

cards.front: How does light reduce the inward dark current of a photoreceptor?
cards.back: Light activates PDE, which breaks down cGMP. CNG channels that cGMP holds open in darkness close, switching off part of the inward current.
cards.quote: Light activates PDE, PDE breaks down cGMP, and channels close.
cards.section: Why a photoreceptor must turn its own gain down

cards.front: Why does closing nearly all outer-segment channels saturate a photoreceptor for further brightening?
cards.back: Almost no inward current remains to switch off, so further brightening cannot produce much additional response.
cards.quote: with almost no current left to switch off, it could not signal any further brightening.
cards.section: Why a photoreceptor must turn its own gain down

cards.front: How can calcium feedback lower photoreceptor gain while preserving the ability to respond on a steady background?
cards.back: It reopens channels to keep current in reserve and trims each new response, so each photon switches off less current for less time.
cards.quote: While the light stays on, the feedback reopens channels, keeping current in reserve, and it cuts and shortens each new response.
cards.section: Why a photoreceptor must turn its own gain down

cards.front: In a photoreceptor, light reduces calcium entry through CNG channels. Suppose outward calcium transport is also stopped during that interval. What happens to the usual calcium decline, and why?
cards.back: The usual decline is prevented through these routes: reduced entry cannot lower calcium by continued extrusion if extrusion has also stopped.
cards.quote: Calcium falls, because entry drops while extrusion continues.
cards.section: The loop: two sensors, two jobs

cards.front: At low outer-segment calcium, {{c1::GCAP1 and GCAP2}} speed cGMP synthesis in photoreceptors.
cards.back: More cGMP helps reopen CNG channels.
cards.quote: GCAP1 and GCAP2, the guanylyl cyclase activating proteins, speed cGMP synthesis;
cards.section: The loop: two sensors, two jobs

cards.front: How does falling calcium affect recoverin-mediated control of visual pigment shutoff?
cards.back: Recoverin releases GRK1, allowing the kinase to shut off activated visual pigment sooner.
cards.quote: Recoverin lets go of GRK1, the kinase that switches off activated visual pigment, so the pigment is shut off sooner.
cards.section: The loop: two sensors, two jobs

cards.front: Mouse rods lacking GCAP1 and GCAP2 have single-photon responses about five times larger than controls and recover slowly. What normal feedback function does this reveal?
cards.back: GCAP feedback normally speeds cGMP restoration as calcium falls, limiting and shortening the response to each photon.
cards.quote: Single-photon responses in rods lacking both GCAPs were about five times larger than in controls, and responses recovered far more slowly.
cards.section: Cut the loop

cards.front: GCAP deletion enlarges a mouse rod’s response in darkness but worsens adaptation on a background. Reconcile these effects using current reserve and gain.
cards.back: Without GCAP feedback, each photon switches off more current for longer in darkness. On a background, less current is recovered, leaving less for later responses. Both follow the rule that feedback trims responses while preserving current reserve.
cards.quote: in darkness only its trimming of each response can show, and on a background its role in holding current in reserve also comes into play.
cards.section: Cut the loop

cards.front: Recoverin normally slows visual pigment shutoff. If recoverin is deleted in mouse rods or cones, what happens to recovery in darkness or on dim backgrounds, and why?
cards.back: Recovery speeds up because recoverin no longer restrains pigment shutoff. This differs from GCAP deletion, which slows cGMP restoration.
cards.quote: in both rods and cones it speeds recovery in darkness and on dim backgrounds, as expected if recoverin normally slows pigment shutoff.
cards.section: Cut the loop

cards.front: Mouse rods and cones still adapt after GCAP1, GCAP2 and recoverin are deleted. What conclusion follows about adaptation mechanisms?
cards.back: These sensors do not explain all adaptation; other mechanisms contribute. Persistence alone does not identify those mechanisms.
cards.quote: When GCAP1, GCAP2 and recoverin are all deleted, mouse rods and cones still show some adaptation, so other mechanisms add to this loop.
cards.section: Cut the loop

cards.front: In the photoreceptor fit S/Sdark = 1/[1 + (I/I0)^n], what background is I0?
cards.back: The background where sensitivity is half its dark value: S/Sdark = 0.5.
cards.quote: I0 is the half-sensitivity background: when I equals I0, the bracket is 1 + 1 and sensitivity is 0.5 of its dark value.
cards.section: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope

cards.front: For S/Sdark = 1/[1 + (I/I0)^n], what is the log-log sensitivity slope when I is well above I0?
cards.back: Approximately −n.
cards.quote: On a log-log plot, at backgrounds well above I0, the curve falls with slope minus n.
cards.section: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope

cards.front: Use S/Sdark = 1/[1 + (I/I0)^n]. At I = 48,800 photons per square micrometre per second, calculate relative sensitivity for control cones (I0 = 48,800, n = 1.0) and GCAP/recoverin-deficient cones (I0 = 12,100, n = 1.5).
cards.back: Control: 1/[1 + (48,800/48,800)^1.0] = 0.500. Deficient: 48,800/12,100 = 4.033; 4.033^1.5 = 8.099; 1/(1 + 8.099) ≈ 0.110. Both are dimensionless fractions of their own dark sensitivity.
cards.quote: Control cones had I0 = 48,800 photons per square micrometre per second and n = 1.0.
cards.section: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope

cards.front: Extrapolate the deficient-cone fit S/Sdark = 1/[1 + (I/12,100)^1.5] from I = 10^6 to 10^7 photons per square micrometre per second. For a small flash of fixed contrast and duration, calculate the ratio of final to initial peak response using (S/Sdark) × I.
cards.back: Let P(I) = I/[1 + (I/12,100)^1.5]. P(10^6) ≈ 1,329.23 and P(10^7) ≈ 420.88 in photons per square micrometre per second. Their dimensionless ratio is 0.3166: about a 3.16-fold decrease. This extrapolates beyond the measured range.
cards.quote: The paper tested backgrounds up to about 400,000, so the 10^6 and 10^7 rows show what the fitted equations do beyond the data, not measurements.
cards.section: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope

cards.front: A photoreceptor has flash sensitivity proportional to 1/background over a range of bright backgrounds. Within that range, double the background while keeping a small flash’s contrast and duration fixed. What happens to its peak response, and why?
cards.back: It stays about the same. Sensitivity halves, but the flash adds twice as many photons. Their product, which determines the peak response, is unchanged.
cards.quote: With S proportional to 1/I, the I cancels, so for a fixed duration the response depends on C alone.
cards.section: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope

cards.front: At one background, control cones retain 0.500 of their dark sensitivity and deficient cones retain 0.110. Can those fractions establish which genotype has greater absolute sensitivity? Explain the missing comparison.
cards.back: No. Absolute sensitivity is each fraction multiplied by that genotype’s dark sensitivity, which is not supplied. The rule is that each curve is normalized to its own dark value; a smaller fraction need not mean a smaller absolute response per photon.
cards.quote: Each sensitivity is normalized to its own genotype's dark sensitivity, so 4.55 is not a ratio of absolute thresholds between genotypes.
cards.section: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope

cards.front: Why does a photoreceptor sensitivity curve falling faster than 1/background not directly measure the remaining current reserve?
cards.back: It measures how flash sensitivity changes with background. A steep fall fits poor current recovery but does not directly quantify the current still flowing.
cards.quote: but the slope alone does not measure how much current is left.
cards.section: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope

cards.front: In GCAP/recoverin-deficient mouse cones, fitted I0 was about a quarter of control and the slope was steeper. Which statistical distinction must accompany that comparison?
cards.back: The I0 shift was not statistically significant; the steeper slope was. The quarter describes central fit values rather than an established shift.
cards.quote: The knockout's quarter is the ratio of central values, 12,100/48,800, about 0.25; unlike that shift, the steeper slope was statistically significant.
cards.section: Reading an adaptation curve: half-sensitivity background and slope

cards.front: Which photoreceptor class mainly serves dim light, and which serves daylight, colour and sharp vision?
cards.back: Rods mainly serve dim light; cones serve daylight, colour and sharp vision.
cards.quote: Rods serve dim light; cones serve daylight, colour and sharp vision.
cards.section: Rods and cones divide the range, and rods in daylight

cards.front: What biochemical contrast helps explain the lower sensitivity and briefer responses of cones in the purified carp rod–cone comparison?
cards.back: Response-generating reactions are somewhat less effective in cones, while response-ending and recovery reactions are much more effective.
cards.quote: the reactions that generate a response are somewhat less effective in cones, while the reactions that end and recover a response are much more effective.
cards.section: Rods and cones divide the range, and rods in daylight

cards.front: In cone-deficient mouse retina, rod-driven contrast responses initially weaken under a bright background, then return during continued exposure. What does the time course imply about a fixed irradiance threshold for permanent rod saturation?
cards.back: It contradicts permanent saturation at that fixed background in this preparation. Rod-driven signalling depends on exposure history as well as irradiance.
cards.quote: Instead, contrast sensitivity recovered with continued exposure, and recovery was faster at higher backgrounds.
cards.section: Rods and cones divide the range, and rods in daylight

cards.front: Mouse ganglion-cell and thalamic responses recover during bright-light exposure, and a phototransduction model implicates gain changes and bleaching. What further observations would strengthen the mechanistic claim and a claim about human daylight vision?
cards.back: Measure rod current during continued bright exposure to test the proposed mechanism directly, then test humans under rod-isolating conditions. The rules are that downstream recordings support a model inference and mouse results alone set no human daylight cutoff.
cards.quote: The recordings came from ganglion cells and thalamus, not rod current, so the gain-and-bleaching account is a model's inference.
cards.section: Rods and cones divide the range, and rods in daylight

cards.front: What information tradeoff accompanies adaptation of rods and cones to changing mean light?
cards.back: They keep reporting contrast across backgrounds while conveying less about absolute light level.
cards.quote: Adaptation lets rods and cones keep reporting contrast as the mean light changes, at the cost of reporting less about the absolute light level.
cards.section: Rods and cones divide the range, and rods in daylight

cards.front: In typical retinitis pigmentosa, which photoreceptors die first, and which loss later threatens central vision?
cards.back: Rods die first; subsequent cone loss threatens central vision.
cards.quote: central vision is lost later, when cones fail
cards.section: A second question: when photoreceptors die

cards.front: How could loss of rod-derived cone viability factor (RdCVF) help explain secondary cone death in retinitis pigmentosa?
cards.back: Cones may lose support for glucose uptake and aerobic glycolysis. This is one experimental candidate; oxidative damage and other causes remain possible.
cards.quote: the pathway increases cone glucose entry and aerobic glycolysis.
cards.section: A second question: when photoreceptors die

cards.front: In a cone-survival model, a mutant RdCVF fails to bind basigin-1, increase glucose uptake or prevent secondary cone death. What mechanism does this support, and what claim remains too strong?
cards.back: It supports a link between RdCVF binding, glucose uptake and cone survival in the model. It does not establish that this pathway is the sole cause of cone death in humans.
cards.quote: A missense mutant failed to bind basigin-1, stimulate glucose uptake or prevent secondary cone death in the model.
cards.section: A second question: when photoreceptors die

cards.front: What does the multi-luminance mobility test used in the RPE65 augmentation trial measure?
cards.back: The dimmest light level at which a person passes a navigation course.
cards.quote: a navigation course scored by the dimmest light level at which the person passes it.
cards.section: Rescuing vision: what two gene-therapy trials can claim

cards.front: A randomized RPE65 augmentation trial with masked outcome grading found a 1.6-light-level between-group difference in mean bilateral mobility change at one year. State the supported efficacy claim with its population and endpoint limits.
cards.back: Treated participants with biallelic RPE65 disease and viable retina improved more than controls on the multi-luminance mobility test at one year. This does not establish benefit across retinal diseases or every visual endpoint.
cards.quote: The mobility claim in the table is limited to participants with biallelic RPE65 disease and viable retina, to the MLMT as an endpoint, and to the follow-up of the trial.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does the randomized RPE65 augmentation trial support a stronger efficacy claim than the single-arm CEP290 editing study, even though CEP290 participants had untreated fellow eyes?
cards.back: Randomized controls and masked grading address shared practice and grader bias. Fellow eyes share participants and testing days but do not match the procedure or eliminate eye differences and expectation. Under these control-design rules, CEP290 supports observed safety and a preliminary benefit signal, rather than an isolated treatment-effect estimate.
cards.quote: the two eyes may differ in disease stage, and expectation can differ between a treated and an untreated eye.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A hypothetical vision study reports that participants improved on at least one of several outcomes. Why is that weaker evidence than improvement on one specified sensitivity endpoint?
cards.back: More outcomes create more opportunities for an improvement. “At least one” also does not mean all outcomes improved; a specified endpoint gives a clearer statement of what changed.
cards.quote: a count of "at least one" rises with the number of outcomes.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A hypothetical vision study must address both practice from repeated testing and grader expectations. What comparison and assessment arrangement would address them, and what bias would remain if participants knew their assignment?
cards.back: Use randomized controls tested on the same schedule and masked outcome graders. Controls address shared practice; masking limits grader bias. Participant expectations would still not be equalized.
cards.quote: Start with what randomization buys: a control group that goes through the same practice and repeated testing, with masked grading limiting grader bias.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Calcium-bound calmodulin lowers a photoreceptor CNG channel’s sensitivity to {{c1::cGMP}}.
cards.back: Lower calcium in light therefore helps channels reopen.
cards.quote: lower the channel's sensitivity to cGMP, so lower calcium in the light helps channels reopen.
cards.section: The third feedback: the channel itself

cards.front: A human GCAP1 variant keeps cyclase active at high calcium. Would a GCAP knockout reproduce this feedback defect, and why?
cards.back: No. The variant keeps cyclase active under an inappropriate calcium condition, whereas a knockout removes GCAP feedback. Distorting feedback and removing it are different perturbations.
cards.quote: most keep the cyclase active when calcium is high, so they distort the feedback rather than remove it.
cards.section: GCAP1 in human disease

cards.front: GCAP/recoverin-deficient mouse cones still adapt in a low-calcium bath. Design a stronger test that a candidate accounts for calcium-independent residual adaptation.
cards.back: Hold outer-segment calcium fixed while running a background series, comparing sensor-deficient cells with and without the candidate. The rule is that bath calcium is not a direct clamp; this proposed clamp has not yet worked in mouse photoreceptors.
cards.quote: A direct test would hold outer-segment calcium fixed while the background series is run in cells lacking each candidate in turn.
cards.section: When the sensors are deleted, some adaptation remains

cards.front: In a human single-photon study, pooled forced-choice performance was 0.516 versus 0.5 chance (P = 0.0545), while selected or combined analyses gave stronger evidence. What interpretation respects both the endpoint and analysis limits?
cards.back: Evidence for single-photon perception is analysis-dependent, rather than proof of reliable awareness of every delivered photon. The rules are to distinguish forced choice from awareness and to track trial selection; the sample also comprised only three men.
cards.quote: So the evidence for single-photon perception is real but analysis-dependent: it comes from three men, it depends on how trials were selected and analysed,
cards.section: One photon: what 1942 showed and what 2016 added

cards.front: Why does recording an electrical response to one absorbed photon in a rod not establish that a person consciously sees one delivered photon?
cards.back: Delivery, rod absorption, the cellular response and perceptual reporting are distinct steps. A rod response alone establishes neither absorption of every delivered photon nor conscious perception.
cards.quote: A rod responding to one photon is not the same as a person seeing one.
cards.section: One photon: what 1942 showed and what 2016 added

cards.front: An engineered photoreceptor-support model retains normal short RdCVF but lacks the long form RdCVFL. Which protective role is directly missing, and why?
cards.back: The long form’s protection against oxidative stress is missing. Short RdCVF supports the glucose-uptake pathway, while RdCVFL provides the described antioxidant support.
cards.quote: RdCVFL, a thioredoxin-fold protein that helps protect photoreceptors against oxidative stress;
cards.section: RdCVF: one gene, two forms
